headline: Powerful Health Panel Has Tumultuous First Meeting With RFK Jr’s Appointees

paragraphs.text: After a year and a half of paralysis, the United States Preventive Services Task Force reconvened on Thursday and Friday for the first time with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s newly appointed members.

It quickly became apparent that a bumpy road lies ahead for the task force, which plays a critical role in Americans’ health care by informing what screenings clinicians recommend and what preventive services insurers are required to cover. It considers topics including mammograms, colonoscopies, H.I.V. prevention medications and much more.

The 16 task force members — eight appointed by Mr. Kennedy in September, and eight predating the current administration — aired significant disagreements on whether they should continue to evaluate evidence through the task force’s traditional processes.
At various points, some new members made comments that suggested they were unfamiliar with those procedures, and with the types of questions the task force seeks to answer.

One, Dr. Louis Wilson, asked what the task force normally did in the virtual meetings its internal work groups hold between its three annual in-person gatherings. And in discussing whether to make a recommendation about screening adolescents for unhealthy alcohol use, two — Dr. Ronald Karlsberg and the new chair, Dr. Seth Corey — made comments that suggested they believed the question at issue was whether teen drinking was healthy, rather than whether there was enough evidence to support the benefits of screening.
In a significant departure from past practice, the task force spent Friday morning listening to presentations from outside experts with financial conflicts of interest.

Conflicts of interest also required three new members to recuse themselves from discussion of a long-delayed cervical cancer screening recommendation. All three were among those who received waivers to serve despite owning stocks in large pharmaceutical and biotech companies, whose products are affected by numerous task force recommendations.

In the past, people with such conflicts were not appointed to the panel to begin with. Very occasionally, someone had to recuse because of a narrow conflict on a single topic, said Dr. Michael Silverstein, the chair of the task force until March. But he could recall that happening only twice in roughly a decade. Three recusals on one topic suggest a body of members “for whom conflicts of interest are going to be a very big problem,” he said.

This was the first in-person meeting since March 2025, after the health department canceled four in a row. While members continued to meet virtually in the intervening time, political appointees prevented them from posting drafts for public comment, voting and publishing final recommendations. Guidelines on at least 18 topics stalled.

On Thursday, Carrie Patnode, a behavioral epidemiologist at Kaiser Permanente, presented the findings of a systematic evidence review her team completed last year for a pending recommendation on lifestyle changes and cardiovascular disease. But she noted that it didn’t incorporate more recent evidence published since the review was completed. Evidence reviews on many topics that stalled over the past year and a half are likely to be similarly out of date.

Perhaps the tensest part of the meeting came when the members discussed edits that Dr. Roger D. Klein, a political appointee leading the federal agency that oversees the task force, had requested to the cervical cancer screening recommendation. These included objections from Dr. Klein to mentioning racial disparities in cervical cancer.
During that conversation, Dr. Sei Lee, a member whose tenure predates Mr. Kennedy, said he wanted to “call out the elephant in the room.”
“I worry that having edits from political leadership on the top line may lead to the perception that the task force recommendations are no longer scientifically independent,” Dr. Lee said.

Ultimately, the task force went into a private session to discuss whether to ratify the recommendation, along with the one on alcohol abuse screening and a third on screening for perinatal depression. The task force’s press office said the vote tallies would be made public, but didn’t say when.

A person who was in the room, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said that after arguments in which Dr. Klein heatedly defended his removal of the mentions of racial disparities, the task force approved the recommendation with its original language. The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Under a June 2025 Supreme Court ruling, Mr. Kennedy has the authority to overrule the task force’s decisions.
